title: UN peacekeeping chief warns of ‘security vacuum’ as Blue Helmets leave Lebanon and Western Sahara

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student and a career advisor discuss a UN internship application.

script.en: Professor Liu, I'm applying for that UN peacekeeping internship in New York, and I'm a bit unsure how to frame my thesis project in the personal statement.
Good timing. The UN is winding down several long-running missions, so they're likely looking for people who can think about transitions, not just patrols. What's your thesis on?
It's about how local communities in conflict zones access humanitarian aid when international forces withdraw. I used two case studies, one in Africa and one in the Middle East.
That's directly relevant. Don't just describe the cases. Show what you found. Did the aid access improve or worsen when the blue helmets left?
In one case it got worse because no neutral actor was left to escort convoys. In the other, local groups took over fairly smoothly, but only after a year of training.
There you go. The UN is worried about a security vacuum right now, so your evidence that transitions can work, given time and preparation, is exactly the kind of nuance they want.
But I don't want to sound like I'm criticizing the UN's withdrawal decisions. I know the Security Council is deadlocked.

You don't have to criticize. Frame it as risk assessment. Say that withdrawal without a follow-on arrangement creates humanitarian costs, and then show the conditions under which those costs can be reduced.
Should I mention the Western Sahara case? The mission there closed after thirty-five years without ever holding the referendum it was meant to organize.

Mention it briefly as a cautionary example, but keep the focus on your own findings. The committee reads hundreds of statements. A clear, evidence-based argument will stand out more than a broad survey.
That makes sense. I'll restructure the statement around my two findings and keep the policy background to two sentences.
Perfect. And send me a draft by Friday. I'll check whether your claims are supported and whether the tone is appropriate for an international organization.

script.en: When a peacekeeping mission closes, the departure of uniformed personnel is only the most visible change. A less noticed but equally consequential shift occurs in the local economy and in the delivery of basic services, where the effects of withdrawal can be felt long after the blue helmets have gone. In many mission areas, UN personnel rent offices and accommodation, buy supplies and employ local staff, and their presence creates a small but steady demand that supports jobs and keeps money circulating in communities that may have few other sources of income. The humanitarian sector is also affected in ways that are often underestimated. Aid agencies often rely on the logistics and security arrangements that peacekeepers provide, and when those arrangements end, convoys may be delayed, and access to remote areas can become more expensive and more dangerous. These effects do not automatically justify keeping a mission in place indefinitely. Critics argue that missions can create dependencies and that host countries must eventually assume responsibility for their own security and services. The difficulty is the timing and the preparation. Where a transition has been planned, local institutions may gradually take over tasks such as escorting aid or monitoring ceasefires. Where it has not, the gap can be filled by armed groups or simply left empty, and civilians bear the cost. Analysts therefore suggest that withdrawal should be treated as a process rather than an event. Planning should begin well before the mandate ends, and it should include funding for local services, training for local partners and a clear political agreement among the parties involved. The lesson is simple to state and hard to apply, and A mission's end is not the end of international responsibility. It is a test of whether the international community can convert a military presence into a durable civilian arrangement.

sections.title: The Cost of Leaving: UN Peacekeeping Withdrawals
sections.passage:
The UN's peacekeeping chief warned on Wednesday that the withdrawal of Blue Helmets from Lebanon and Western Sahara risks leaving a dangerous security vacuum, while the Security Council remains divided over what, if anything, should replace them. The warning came as the organization prepares to lose some of its longest-standing military deployments.

The UN mission in Western Sahara closed on 31 October after 35 years. In Lebanon, the peacekeeping force that has patrolled the border with Israel since 1978 is due to cease operations at the end of the year. Around 7,500 peacekeepers are still serving with the UN Interim Force in Lebanon, acting as a go-between for the Lebanese and Israeli armies, monitoring violations and helping humanitarian aid get through.

Mr. Lacroix, the peacekeeping chief, has just returned from Lebanon. He said President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam had told him they feared a security vacuum once the peacekeepers leave, with no one left to stop border incidents from turning into clashes. There is a humanitarian cost too. He offered a cautious estimate that about 10,000 people are still living between the Blue Line and the forward defence line Israel has set up inside Lebanese territory, and their access to aid depends heavily on the mission.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres put forward options in June, but the Security Council has yet to agree on any follow-on arrangement. Mr. Lacroix urged council members to decide what form a future international presence could take. The same deadlock has already ended the UN's presence in Western Sahara. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara shut down on 31 October after council members failed to agree on renewing its mandate.

Russia vetoed a United States draft that would have reshaped the mission around a solution based on autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty. A rival Russian text calling for a one-year renewal fell short of the nine votes needed to pass. The mission was set up in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front. It never held the self-determination referendum it was created to organize, and hostilities in the territory resumed in 2020. Mr. Lacroix confirmed that the mission was now in its liquidation phase.

Elsewhere, in the Golan, UN observers were receiving complaints from civilians about detentions, movement restrictions and property seizures linked to the Israeli military presence. In Abyei, the territory disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, recent drone attacks have highlighted another growing danger. Blue Helmets are having to adapt to technologies that put both their own personnel and the civilians they protect at risk. The UN is reviewing its military and technological capabilities, but Mr. Lacroix said the answer could not be purely technical. Above all, he said, it was a matter of political responsibility.

long_sentences.en: The UN’s peacekeeping chief warned on Wednesday that the withdrawal of “Blue Helmets” from Lebanon and Western Sahara risks leaving a dangerous security vacuum, while the Security Council remains divided over what, if anything, should replace them.

Briefing journalists at UN Headquarters in New York, Mr. Lacroix said the organization was losing some of its longest-standing military deployments, with no guarantee that the countries concerned could maintain stability on their own.

He said President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam had told him they feared a “security vacuum” once the peacekeepers leave, with no one left to stop border incidents from turning into clashes.
